To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the proportion of telephone queries and/or appointment changes was higher in the 50–64 age group (29.7%) compared with the 65–69 age group (26.5%) but that the main reason for changing an appointment was inconvenience for both groups.
The proportion of women who made a telephone query about the date and time of the appointment was significantly higher among women aged 50 to 64 than women aged 65 to 69.

a study of the number of queries or changes in appointments arising from a demonstration project to extend screening to older women.
the number of appointment queries or requests for change of appointment in a demonstration study of extending the NHS breast screening programme to women aged 65-69.

extending breast cancer screening to women aged 65-69 does not increase the administrative costs of the programme.
the administrative cost of extending the breast screening program to older women is not greater than the cost of inviting younger women.

the cost of extending the breast screening age to 69 years would not increase significantly.
the administrative costs associated with extending breast screening to 65–69 year olds are similar to those for women aged 55–64 years.
extending the breast screening age range from 50–64 to 50–69 years does not result in a higher number of queries or appointment changes than the existing screening age group.

extending the breast screening age to 70 years will not increase the number of appointment queries or appointment changes.
